name: null-object
intent: Provide a surrogate collaborator that implements the same interface as the real one but does nothing, so callers can keep using the collaborator unconditionally instead of repeating a null test at every call site.
problem: A collaborator is optional by design - a logger that was not injected, a listener that was never registered, a query that legitimately yields nothing, a feature that is switched off - yet every call site repeats the same guard. The duplicated null checks dominate the surrounding logic, one forgotten guard crashes with a null dereference, and the do-nothing outcome, which is identical for every caller, is re-implemented in each of them.
context: Object-oriented designs whose collaborator may be absent as a normal state and whose neutral behaviour is well defined: logging, notification, metrics, strategies, listeners, empty result sets. Applies when the interface can be implemented without side effects and when no caller needs to distinguish 'absent' from 'present but neutral'.
benefits: Callers lose the branch: real and absent collaborators are used through one interface, so null tests, safe-navigation guards and duplicated do-nothing code disappear from the calling sites (Woolf: client code becomes simple and uniform).
The do-nothing behaviour has exactly one home, so its semantics stay consistent across all clients and can be changed centrally (for example turning a discard sink into a counting sink).

The relationship becomes mandatory (1 instead of 0..1): fields and parameters can be declared non-nullable, which removes a whole class of null-dereference defects and documents the contract at the type level.
Tests that do not care about the collaborator can run against the null instance without configuring a logging framework, a broker or a database.

A stateless null instance is immutable and therefore safely shareable (and thread-safe), so it can be a const/static singleton with no per-call allocation, and it composes with Singleton and Flyweight.
tradeoffs: One extra class per interface: every abstract collaborator that needs a neutral form gains a null implementation, and each new interface method must be implemented there too; when the null object subclasses the real class instead of implementing an interface, a forgotten override silently inherits real behaviour (Kerievsky's maintenance liability).

Absence becomes invisible: a null object makes a missing dependency look like success - discarded log lines, dropped notifications, ignored orders - so mis-wiring surfaces late, in production, or never.

It forces uniformity: all clients must agree on what 'do nothing' means; when they disagree, the null class either grows pluggable state or multiplies into several null classes - the class explosion Woolf lists as a consequence.
A null object never becomes a real object, so late binding needs a Proxy, a setter or a registry, and code that expects 'absent until configured' semantics must change shape.

Special-case leakage: identity comparisons, serialization and any isNull()/type query re-introduce the conditional the pattern removed, and a null instance that is accidentally mutable becomes shared global state.
It hides the wiring question rather than answering it: a system can ship with the real collaborator never installed, and only the null object running.

participants.responsibility: Uses the AbstractObject interface and calls it unconditionally; it must not need to know whether the receiver is the real or the null implementation.
Declares the interface (and any default behaviour) that both the real and the null implementation satisfy, so the two are substitutable.
Concrete implementation providing the useful behaviour the client expects.

Provides an interface identical to AbstractObject's and implements every request with neutral behaviour; stateless and shared, and several null classes exist when 'do nothing' means different things to different clients.

use_cases: Libraries that accept an optional logger: install a shared no-op logger by default so the library never null-tests and callers configure logging only at the composition root (Python logging.NullHandler, Java LogManager.NullHandler, .NET System.Diagnostics.TraceSource, Go log.New(io.Discard, ...)).
Event and input dispatch: a widget or actor with no registered handler holds a do-nothing handler, so the dispatch loop needs no 'if (handler)' branch.
Features that are switched off: a disabled cache, queue, metrics sink or rate limiter is replaced by a neutral implementation instead of threading 'if (enabled)' through the domain logic.

Empty results: return an empty collection, iterator or stream instead of null so callers iterate unconditionally (Python [], Collections.emptyList(), Java Stream.empty(), Go []T{}, .NET Enumerable.Empty<T>()).
Domain special cases: an unknown or anonymous principal ('guest', Fowler's 'occupant') that answers the same protocol with neutral values instead of forcing a null check into every domain rule.
Test isolation: an inert collaborator replaces a mock when the test asserts on the subject's own behaviour and the interaction is irrelevant.
Batch and ETL pipelines: a null sink on a branch whose output is intentionally discarded keeps the pipeline shape uniform.

Optional context managers: Python's contextlib.nullcontext(None) wraps an optional with-block in a do-nothing manager so callers use 'with resource or nullcontext():' uniformly (Python 3.7+, equivalent to ExitStack in older versions).
Stream and reader/writer sinks: Go's io.Discard (zero-value *io.discard), Python's os.devnull, .NET's Stream.Null - all null objects for I/O that silently absorb bytes.
Configuration and settings: a NullConfig that returns default/zero values for every key, keeping the calling code free of has_key() branches.
Async execution contexts: a NullExecutor or NullScheduler that schedules tasks but never runs them, useful for testing or when async work must be explicitly deferred.
Strategy and policy objects: a NullEncryption, NullCompression or NullCache that documents the 'opt-out' policy in the type system rather than a null reference.

NestJS and DI-based frameworks: register either a real service (ConsoleLoggerService) or a null service (NullLoggerService) as the LoggerService provider in the module; the service layer injects and calls the interface without any conditional logic, and tests override only the provider they care about.

TypeScript/Node.js plugin systems: use a Proxy-based null object (e.g., @wherejuly/null-object npm package) as a type-safe no-op fallback when an optional plugin is not installed, so the host application calls plugin methods unconditionally.

C++ template policy form: make the null behaviour a template policy parameter; the compiler eliminates no-op calls entirely at compile time with zero runtime overhead on hot paths (used for zero-allocation logging and metrics in game engines and HFT systems).

Reactive Subject/Observer dispatch: a Subject holds a collection of Observer pointers; each observer slot defaults to Observer::null() so the notify loop iterates unconditionally without null guards, making the slot lifecycle irrelevant to the dispatch logic.

Builder pattern defaults: a RequestBuilder whose optional fields (logger, cache, metrics) default to null objects lets clients build a fully-functional instance without configuring every collaborator; each optional collaborator can be overridden selectively.
Middleware and pipeline chains: an optional audit middleware is replaced by a null-object middleware so the middleware chain iterates uniformly without 'if (enabled)' branching at each stage.

ORM/JPA entity associations: a missing optional entity (e.g., an Order with no assigned Shipment) can hold a NullShipment stand-in so the domain code navigates the association without null checks; the getter/setter must prevent Hibernate from persisting the null object.

Java applications that need an OutputStream but intentionally discard bytes can use Apache Commons IO's NullOutputStream.INSTANCE; it preserves the OutputStream contract while centralizing the no-op sink instead of branching at each writer.

VisualWorks Smalltalk GUI and compiler components can use Woolf's NoController and NullScope as collaborators for read-only views or outermost scopes, preserving the Controller/NameScope protocol while making input or lookup a deliberate no-op.

The ADAPTIVE Service eXecutive (ASX) C++ framework's Null_Mutex supplies acquire/release operations that do nothing for single-threaded services, preserving the mutex strategy interface without paying locking overhead.
avoid_when: Absence carries information the caller must act on (an unknown user that must be rejected, a missing price that must be reported) - use an option type (Rust Option, Java Optional, Kotlin/Swift/TypeScript nullable) or a queryable Special Case.
The missing collaborator indicates a configuration or wiring bug - a null audit log, a null payment processor or a null database should fail fast with an exception or a Result, not succeed silently.
The guard is local and cheap: one call site, or a language with safe navigation (a?.b, x ?? default) - the operator is simpler than a new type.

The interface contract promises an effect (send, persist, charge, authorise) and a neutral implementation would violate it; Liskov substitution makes a 'null' implementation of such an interface a defect.
Callers must distinguish 'absent' from 'present and empty' (404 vs empty list, missing key vs empty string) - a null object erases the distinction.
The collaborator is expected to appear later: use a Proxy, a registry or a setter, because a null object never turns into a real one.

The language has sum-type Option/Maybe that encodes absence in the type system and forces handling at every call site - Rust Option, Scala Option, Haskell Maybe - prefer the native type over a hand-rolled null object, though a null object still makes sense when collaborators must be called uniformly (trait object, DI).
anti_patterns: Silent-success null object: a no-op implementation of a collaborator whose absence matters (audit log, billing, authorisation), so the system reports success while nothing happened.
Half-migrated null object: the factory sometimes returns the null instance and sometimes null, so both code paths survive and the reference stays nullable.
Type-querying clients: 'if (customer.isNull())', 'x instanceof NullCustomer' or 'x === NullObject' - the conditional the pattern was meant to remove returns in a different syntax.

Mutating pseudo-null: a null object that switches to real behaviour at run time, or that carries per-client configuration of what 'nothing' means; that is a Proxy or a State, and Woolf explicitly excludes it from this pattern.
NotImplementedException null: a 'null' implementation that throws on some of the interface's methods, breaking substitutability and surfacing an unrelated exception type.
Null object as production double: shipping the test stand-in (or a NullLogger) on a path where the real collaborator must run.
Option-wrapped null object: wrapping a null object in Option/Nullable creates two encodings of absence (None and NullObject) that different call sites read differently, defeating the uniformity goal.

ORM-persisted null object: a null entity object (e.g., NullShipment) is set on a JPA/Hibernate association and accidentally persisted to the database with all fields null or zero, corrupting data; prevent this by handling the null object in the entity getter/setter or annotating the field @Transient.

Mutable shared null object: a null object with writable state (a counter, a flag, a lazily-computed default) is shared across concurrent clients and its state becomes order-dependent; a null object must be immutable to be safely shared.

Default method inheritance: adding a default method to an interface is silently inherited by a null object subclass that was implemented by overriding only the original methods — the null object accidentally gains real behaviour.
design_principles: Liskov substitution: the null implementation must honour the interface's contract - neutral results have to satisfy the same postconditions and invariants as the real one.
Polymorphic dispatch instead of conditionals: the absence test moves from every client into a type (Tell, Don't Ask).
Dependency inversion and interface segregation: clients depend on the abstract collaboration, which both the real and the null implementation satisfy.
Single responsibility and DRY: 'do nothing' is one encapsulated responsibility with one implementation instead of duplicated guard code.
Explicit failure policy: choosing graceful degradation over fail-fast is a decision that must be made deliberately, interface by interface.
Open/closed: new neutral behaviours arrive as new null classes, never as edits to client code.
Fail-fast for critical paths: audit, billing and authorisation collaborators should never be null objects - absence there is a wiring defect, not a feature flag.
best_practices: Make the null instance a shared immutable singleton (const/static/object/enum value) and expose it through a named accessor (Logger::null(), NullLogger.Instance, io.Discard, NoOpListener) so callers stop hand-rolling nulls.
Implement the null object against an interface rather than by subclassing the real class, so newly added methods cannot be silently inherited.

Declare collaborator fields and parameters non-nullable and initialise them with the null instance at the earliest possible point (constructor default, field initialiser, factory fallback), so no path leaves a real null behind.
Keep the neutral implementation stateless and side-effect free - no logging, counters or lazy state except the deliberate discard - so it can be shared across threads.
Never require callers to detect the null object: where a caller must distinguish absent from present, the collaboration needs an option value or a real special case instead.
Test both paths: assert that callers behave identically with the real and the null collaborator, and add one wiring test proving the real collaborator is installed in production.
Keep null objects off security- and money-critical paths (audit, authorisation, billing) and fail fast there.

Prefer the language's native Option/Maybe type (Rust Option, Scala Option, Kotlin nullable, Swift Optional) over a hand-rolled null object when the type system enforces handling; use the null object when collaborators must be called uniformly through a shared interface or trait object.
Use null objects at the composition root (entry point, factory, DI container) to set defaults, not scattered through domain code - the null instance is a deployment-time decision, not a runtime one.

When multiple neutral behaviours are needed for the same interface, prefer several named null classes (NullLogger, CountingLogger, DiscardLogger) over a single null class with pluggable configuration.
Name null objects explicitly after what they do rather than what they are: NullLogger, NoOpListener, DiscardSink - not GenericNullObject.

In Java, prefer enum singletons for stateless null objects (e.g., enum NoOpLogger implements Logger { INSTANCE }) — they are thread-safe, serialisation-safe and reflection-resistant without boilerplate.

Use a StrictNull variant in tests — a null object that throws on any call — to enforce by construction that no interaction with the optional collaborator occurs on a given code path; a future accidental call surfaces immediately instead of silently doing nothing.

Expose three null-object tiers for testing: inert (does nothing, used when the test ignores the collaborator), counting (records calls for assertions, used when the test needs to verify interaction frequency), and strict (throws, used when the test must prove zero interaction occurred).

In languages with dynamic Proxy support (Java java.lang.reflect.Proxy, TypeScript/JS with Proxy, C# with DispatchProxy), a single generic proxy-based null object can handle any interface at runtime without generating a class per interface — useful in plugin systems and dynamically-composed objects.

When using null objects in an ORM or JPA context, ensure they are never accidentally persisted: handle the mapping in the entity getter/setter (return NullObject.INSTANCE from the getter, never let Hibernate see the null object as a managed entity) or mark the field @Transient.

For event-dispatch and Observer patterns, wrap multiple optional handlers in a CompositeHandler that iterates unconditionally over its entries — each handler is either a real handler or a null object that no-ops; the composite never branches on 'is handler present'.

Use null objects in Builder and factory defaults: a builder whose optional collaborators default to null objects (NullLogger, NullCache, NullMetrics) produces a working instance immediately with no conditional branching in clients, and each collaborator can be overridden selectively.

In middleware chains and pipeline patterns, insert a null object as the 'disabled' sentinel for an optional middleware stage so the chain iterates uniformly without 'if (stageEnabled)' guards at each step.

Log or metric null object usage in debug mode at the composition root so accidental mis-wiring — real collaborator never installed — surfaces as observable output rather than silent production behaviour.
Increment the version field when adding or changing the canonical null implementation to signal a schema/API change in the pattern record.
